slides.title: Title
slides.notes: Open the lecture by shifting attention from ordinary functions to relations with many possible outputs. The central move is to stop asking whether one arrow is linear and instead ask whether the whole graph in input-output space is a convex cone. That graph perspective is what makes images, inverse processes, and algebraic operations manageable.

slides.title: Set-Valued Maps
slides.notes: Spend a minute making the notation feel concrete. For a usual function, the vertical fiber over an input contains one point. For a set-valued map, that fiber can be an interval, a cone, or any other set. The graph collects all allowed input-output pairs and becomes the place where convex structure is tested.

slides.title: Graph Cone
slides.notes: This is the main definition slide. The important point is that the cone property lives in product space, not separately in the input and output coordinates. Once two graph points are allowed, every nonnegative linear combination of the two pairs must also be allowed. That single condition packages positive homogeneity and convex additivity.

slides.title: Wedge Model
slides.notes: Use the wedge as the reliable running example. The fibers are vertical intervals, but the graph is the triangular cone between two rays. Scaling an input from one to two scales the whole interval of outputs. This makes the formal definition visible without requiring a high-dimensional example.

slides.title: Process Images
slides.notes: Images are where set-valued notation pays off. For an ordinary map, the image of C is the collection of all values f of x. For a process, every input contributes a whole fiber, so the image is a union of sets. The graph-cone closure explains why cone-shaped input families produce cone-shaped output families.

slides.title: Inverse Process
slides.notes: The inverse process should feel less exotic than it first appears. It asks for all inputs that could have produced a chosen output. In graph language, nothing is recomputed; the two coordinates are exchanged. Because a coordinate flip preserves conic convexity, the inverse process stays inside the same algebraic category.

slides.title: Process Algebra
slides.notes: This slide connects the section back to the algebra of convex sets and bifunctions. Positive scaling of a process scales each output fiber, while addition combines two output fibers at the same input. The reason these operations preserve convex processes is not a new trick; it is the same graph-cone closure applied to the resulting pairs.

slides.title: Closure Check
slides.notes: Tie this directly to the notebook's executable invariant. The point is not that three samples prove the theorem. The point is that the theorem's obligations become inspectable: combine two graph points with nonnegative weights, or scale one graph point, and check that the resulting pair stays in the same wedge. This is a useful guard against sign and coordinate mistakes.

slides.title: Failure Modes
slides.notes: Use this slide to prevent overgeneralization. A process is not certified by nice-looking fibers alone. Boundary pairs, sign restrictions, and input alignment all matter. The product-space graph catches these failures because every algebraic step becomes a concrete membership question for a pair rather than a vague visual impression.

slides.title: Recap
slides.notes: Close by returning to the workflow. A convex process is best remembered as a cone of feasible input-output pairs. Fibers tell us what outputs are possible for a fixed input, images collect reachable outputs, the inverse flips the relation, and process algebra works because positive scaling and addition preserve the graph cone.
